book: 275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life

chapters.relation: In this Foreword, hunter and nature writer David Petersen argues that hunting is his best 'philosophy professor,' teaching lessons about life, death, and human animality. He casts predation and evasion as a 'sacred game' that sculpted prey species through natural selection, and invokes Aldo Leopold's ideal of restraint 'even when no one is watching' to distinguish true, process-oriented hunters from gadget-reliant 'Wannabee' shooters using bait stations, GPS, and motorized decoys. He warns that banning hunting would cause wildlife overpopulation, framing the human as an ambivalent predator: both 'good' and 'bad.'

Editor Nathan Kowalsky's introduction opens with his boyhood memory of his father shooting a whitetail buck and his own tears, using it to argue that hunting confronts us with life and death 'right there in front of your face.' He insists hunting and philosophy are not an oxymoron (mocking the Elmer Fudd stereotype against Socrates 'downtown'), casts hunting itself as a paradox worth philosophizing about, and previews all the volume's chapters, framing philosophy as 'thinking hard' about an activity that makes humans and wildness literally touch through death.

Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.

Opening with his intimate encounter with a wolf, Vitali argues that 'fair chase' cannot mean fairness to the animal — since a right to fair chase would imply a more basic right not to be hunted, conceding the anti-hunting case. Instead, invoking Aristotelian human flourishing and Leopold's land ethic, he relocates fair chase to the hunter: hunting is moral only if it serves the biotic community through conservation and lets the hunter enter the predator-prey life-death continuum. He illustrates self-handicapping through master hunter Milo Burcham stalking a distant muley with a recurve bow.

Kretz systematically attacks the claim that hunting is environmental, using the Ducks Unlimited Canada case. She wields Hume's is-ought gap to deny that 'natural' hunting is thereby moral, cites evidence that hunters remove the fittest breeders and eliminate predators, and rejects Thoreau's hope that young hunters 'outgrow' killing as counterproductive (analogous to teaching theft to prevent it). Drawing on Brian Luke, she presses 'the paradox of ethical hunting': the sportsman's code (quick kills, retrieve the wounded) shows concern for the animal that, fully realized, entails not hunting at all.

Cerulli narrates his path from vegan to deer hunter, arguing that the same ethic — the intent to 'do no harm,' rooted in compassion, ahimsa, and feminist critiques of domination — underlies both vegetarianism and his hunting. Confronting the animal deaths hidden behind organic agriculture (farmer Joey 'plugging' deer and smoke-bombing woodchucks), he invokes Carol Adams's 'absent referent' to explain why he had to face the killing directly. Shooting and butchering a buck himself, guided by his Buddhist friend Richard, becomes an act of integrity and refusal of 'forgetfulness.'

Clark analyzes Disney's Bambi as anti-hunting art, showing how the animators used music and the Kantian sublime — keeping Man and Death offscreen, 'felt rather than seen' — to make viewers feel hunting is cosmic murder, while the cute cartoon animals stay merely 'seen.' He then critiques Matt Cartmill, who dissolves hunting by using science and utilitarianism to erase the Man/Nature split (making hunting indistinguishable from murder), faulting Cartmill for flattening life and rejecting the sublime. He resolves the tension via Richard Nelson's The Island Within and Koyukon hunting, which honors continuity and the sublime without a Man/Nature dichotomy.

Seitz gives an existential-phenomenological meditation on hunting's essence, leaning on Ortega y Gasset's Meditations on Hunting: 'one does not hunt in order to kill; on the contrary, one kills in order to have hunted.' Using his daughter Sabina's squirrel-versus-grouse reasoning and his own pronghorn stalks, he argues meat is the 'sign' but not the essence, and (via Heidegger) that hunting is 'a mode of revealing.' Contrasting Marx and Heidegger on technology with Ortega's claim that hunting 'cannot progress,' he frames the hunter as 'natural/prehistoric man' annihilating historical time — a vanishing figure in a climate-changed, thirsty future.

Acton draws on her anthropological fieldwork riding to hounds in English foxhound packs to explore the human/equine partnership with the 'made hunter' horse. Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the body-in-movement and Tim Ingold's notion of 'dwelling,' she argues the rider experiences the hunt through 'muscular consciousness' and 'centaur hours,' taking on the horse's senses and physicality. Trusting the sharp horse to 'work it out' — as when her hunter checked pace to avoid a collision at a jump — becomes an embodied, timeless collaboration binding rider, horse, hounds, and landscape.

Wawatie and Pyne present a traditional Algonquin Anishinabe philosophy of hunting in which all creation — humans, animals, plants, water, rocks — belongs to one family bound by spirit, and hunting is a reciprocal relationship of gift, gratitude, and non-waste rather than a contest. Through Kokom Lena Nottaway's creation story (animals gifting a foggy figure wisdom, vision, strength until humans take form) and the life of 'Nathan' learning the moose, they show hunting as 'a quest for understanding.' A hunting song teaches by indirect clues, letting the learner reach their own awareness, and feast ceremonies honor the prey's sacrifice.

Marvin, a social anthropologist, argues that for 'nature hunters' (Kellert's typology) a taxidermy trophy is not a dead animal but a living souvenir — un recuerdo — that enshrines the memory of a fair-chase hunt. Using Susan Stewart on the souvenir's part/whole incompleteness and Appadurai on value as 'difficulty of acquisition,' he shows how the lethal shot, the pose-reversed photograph, and the taxidermist's craft convert a wild animal into a personal memento that only lives through the hunter's narrative. How the animal was killed (ethically, authentically) matters more than that it was killed; the trophy is the hunter's self-awarded token of ethical excellence.

Geist, a conservation biologist, argues from physiology (elastin-digesting enzymes, B12 need), athletics (one-legged balancing for stalking, precision throwing), and the herbivore-like pattern of human speciation that humans evolved as hunters — a 'carnivorous herbivore.' He contends morality itself was born from hunting: because tools-as-weapons (clubs, spears) let an aggressor kill without retaliation, escaping natural selection's check, early humans had to invent social taboos distinguishing right from wrong. He contrasts Neanderthal 'rodeo' close-quarters spearing with Cro-Magnon distance throwing, linking spear-tracking to endurance running, language, and art — concluding that questioning hunting's morality questions our humanity.

holes.name: Fair Chase
holes.what: The hunting ethic requiring a balance that lets prey generally elude the hunter, with voluntary limits on technology and a duty of a clean, confident kill.
holes.why: Chapter 2 (Vitali) is centrally about redefining what makes fair chase 'fair' and no existing taxonomy concept (land-ethic, animal-rights, virtue-ethics) names this specific hunting-ethics doctrine that recurs across the volume.
